62	def print_table(results, uniform_ppl, grid_best_ppl):

55	def extract_ppl_from_trainer_state(exp_dir: Path) -> float | None:
56	    """Fallback: get last eval_loss from trainer_state.json, convert to ppl."""
57	    candidates = sorted(exp_dir.glob("checkpoint-*/trainer_state.json"))

66	        eval_entries = [e for e in log_history if "eval_loss" in e]
67	        if not eval_entries:

\subsection{Robustness and Boundary Conditions}
\label{sec:robustness}

Across three seeds at $\rho = 0.6$, adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.731 \pm 0.004$) outperforms uniform on in-distribution PPL ($17.763 \pm 0.008$, $\Delta{=}{-}0.032$, paired $t{=}{-}9.95$, $p{=}0.010$\footnote{Computed from 3dp-rounded per-seed values (Table~\ref{tab:rho06}) for reproducibility. Under full-family Bonferroni--Holm correction ($k{=}9$), $p_{\mathrm{BH}}{=}0.064$; directionally consistent across all seeds.}), exceeding the $\rho{=}0.4$ improvement ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$).
The ablation hierarchy is preserved (Grid 17.634\footnote{Single seed; full per-seed results in Appendix~\ref{app:rho06}.} ${<}$ Adaptive 17.731 ${<}$ Uniform 17.763 ${\approx}$ ESS-only 17.763 ${<}$ Random 17.861), but the ESS-only/uniform gap collapses to effectively zero (three-seed means both $17.763$) as ESS binding rises to ${\sim}$49\%.
Random remains substantially worse than uniform (gap 0.098, $\sigma{=}0.025$): detector signal is load-bearing even when the stability constraint dominates; the adaptive method's continued advantage is driven by the $\aeff$ quality constraint, which operates independently of the ESS ceiling.
Three-seed paired comparison confirms $\tau{=}0.7$ outperforms $\tau{=}0.8$ on both holdout and OOD metrics (\S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Scale.}
At 1.7B parameters (Qwen3-1.7B, $\rho{=}0.4$, $\tau{=}0.8$, 3 seeds), the method scales without degradation but the benefit diminishes.
Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves holdout PPL $13.26$ vs.\ uniform $13.27$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.013$); OOD results are partially consistent (OWT $\Delta{=}{-}0.008$, Wiki $\Delta{=}{+}0.013$) and downstream is unchanged ($\Delta{\approx}{+}0.002$), consistent with larger models being more robust to 0.6B-generated contamination.
\paragraph{Out-of-distribution evaluation.}
To test whether the in-distribution improvement reflects distribution matching, we evaluate all three from-scratch seeds on OpenWebText and Wikipedia.
At $\rho{=}0.4$, adaptive reweighting improves 3-seed mean PPL on all three evaluation domains: FineWeb $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, OpenWebText $\Delta{=}{-}0.028$, Wikipedia $\Delta{=}{-}0.029$ (downstream accuracy identical at 0.5414).
OOD improvements exceed the in-distribution gain, indicating genuine quality improvement rather than distribution matching toward the training mixture ($\tau{=}0.8$'s OOD effect is smaller; $\tau{=}0.7$'s advantage reflects active OOD improvement, \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Calibration, not just discrimination.}
Replacing TF-IDF+LR with generative perplexity detectors reverses the advantage across three seeds (GPT-2: AUC\,=\,0.91, ECE\,=\,0.131, $\Delta{=}{+}0.098$; N-gram: AUC\,=\,0.73, ECE\,=\,0.069, $\Delta{=}{+}0.129$; Appendix~\ref{app:detector}).
The TF-IDF vs.\ GPT-2 contrast (comparable AUC, $2.7{\times}$ ECE gap) isolates calibration as an empirically observed requirement in our self-contamination setting; N-gram's better ECE (0.069) does not compensate for insufficient AUC (0.73), confirming that both discrimination and calibration are required.


\subsection{Hyperparameter Sensitivity}
\label{sec:sensitivity}

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
$\tau{=}0.7$ outperforms $\tau{=}0.8$ on holdout at both contamination levels ($\rho{=}0.4$: 17.674 vs.\ 17.683; $\rho{=}0.6$: paired $t{=}{-}4.70$, $p{<}0.05$; \S\ref{sec:robustness}) and achieves larger OOD gains ($\rho{=}0.4$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.028$/$-$0.029 vs.\ $-$0.005/$-$0.009; Table~\ref{tab:tau}, Appendix~\ref{app:tau_rho}).
$\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ all improve holdout over uniform, while $\tau {>} 0.8$ degrades (Appendix~\ref{app:tau_sweep}).

\paragraph{ESS floor $\nmin$.}
The default $\nmin{=}2$ ($\nmin/B{=}0.5$) is optimal; extremes degrade ($\nmin{=}1$: PPL 17.789; $\nmin{=}B$: recovers uniform).
Under $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ coupling, the adaptive advantage monotonically increases across $B \in \{4, 8, 16\}$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.020{\pm}0.008$ (3 seeds), $-$0.050 (2-seed mean), and $-$0.068${\pm}$0.005 (3 seeds), corresponding to $1.0{\times}$, $2.5{\times}$, and $3.4{\times}$ amplification ($p{<}0.01$ at $B{=}16$).
The gap to grid-best narrows from 0.040 ($B{=}4$) to 0.009 ($B{=}16$, seed\,42).

\paragraph{Constraint regime.}
\label{sec:regime}
Over 24{,}412 micro-batches (seed\,42), 5.8\% are clean ($\aeff(0) \geq \tau$, $\bstar{=}0$), 50.9\% are $\aeff$-binding (quality constraint dominates), and 43.3\% are ESS-binding (stability constraint dominates); the distribution is stable across seeds (CV ${<}2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:regime}).
The $\aeff$-binding majority indicates that detector quality signal---not training stability---is the primary bottleneck, reinforcing the calibration requirement (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).

2	\label{app:proofs}

4	\begin{proposition}[$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ monotonicity]
5	\label{prop:monotone}
6	$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b)$ is non-decreasing in $b$, and strictly increasing whenever the batch contains at least one sample with $q_i \in (0,1)$ and $r_i$ is not constant.
7	\end{proposition}
8	
9	\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}]
10	Let $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^b$, $W(b) = \sum_{j=1}^B w_j(b)$, and $\pi_i(b) = w_i(b) / W(b)$.
11	Then
12	\begin{equation*}
13	  \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) = \sum_{i=1}^{B} \pi_i(b)\, r_i,
14	\end{equation*}
15	where $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates whether sample $i$ is real.
16	Taking the derivative with respect to $b$:
17	\begin{align*}
18	  \frac{d\pi_i}{db}
19	  &= \pi_i \!\left(\frac{d \ln w_i}{db} - \frac{d \ln W}{db}\right) \\
20	  &= \pi_i \!\left(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \textstyle\sum_j \pi_j \ln(1{-}q_j)\right).
21	\end{align*}
22	Substituting,
23	\begin{align*}
24	  \frac{d\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}}{db}
25	  &= \sum_i r_i\, \pi_i \!\left(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ln(1{-}q)]\right) \\
26	  &= \mathrm{Cov}_{\pi}\!\bigl(r_i,\, \ln(1{-}q_i)\bigr).
27	\end{align*}
28	Since $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$, the indicator $r_i$ and $\ln(1{-}q_i)$ are positively associated by construction, so the covariance is non-negative.
29	\end{proof}

31	\begin{proposition}[ESS monotonicity]
32	\label{prop:ess_mono}
33	$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ is non-increasing in $b$, and strictly decreasing whenever the batch contains at least two samples with distinct $q$-values.
34	\end{proposition}
35	
36	\begin{proof}
37	Write $\mathrm{ESS}(b) = 1 / \sum_i \pi_i(b)^2$, where $\pi_i(b) = w_i(b) / W(b)$.
38	The denominator $\sum_i \pi_i^2$ is the Herfindahl index $H$.
39	Differentiating $H$ with respect to $b$:
40	\begin{equation*}
41	  \frac{dH}{db} = 2 \sum_i \pi_i^2 \bigl(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ln(1{-}q)]\bigr).
42	\end{equation*}
43	Since $\pi_i \propto (1{-}q_i)^b$, larger $\pi_i$ implies larger $\ln(1{-}q_i)$; the $\pi^2$-weighted sum assigns greater mass to terms where $\ln(1{-}q_i) > \mathbb{E}_\pi[\ln(1{-}q)]$, so $dH/db \geq 0$, with strict inequality when at least two $q$-values differ.
44	Thus $H$ is non-decreasing and $\mathrm{ESS} = 1/H$ is non-increasing.
45	This is a standard property of exponential tilting~\citep{kish1965survey,owen2013mc}.
46	\end{proof}

1	Let $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}$ denote a pretraining corpus with token-level contamination ratio $\rho = |\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}| / |\mathcal{D}|$, assumed unknown~\citep{cheng2025contamination}.
2	A detector assigns each sample $x$ a synthetic probability $q(x) \in [0,1]$; following \citet{drayson2025detection}, we weight each sample as $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^{b}$, where $b \geq 0$ is a sharpening exponent ($b{=}0$ recovers uniform training).
3	Rather than selecting $b$ via grid search~\citep{drayson2025detection}, we derive $b$ per-batch from the batch's $q$-score distribution using two opposing constraints.
4	
5	Given a batch $\mathcal{B} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_B\}$ with scores $q_i = q(x_i)$ and weights $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^{b}$:
6	
7	\paragraph{Quality floor.}
8	Let $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$ indicate likely-real samples. The \emph{effective real proportion} $\aeff(b) = \sum_i w_i(b) r_i / \sum_i w_i(b)$ measures weight allocated to real samples.
9	We require $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$, yielding a lower bound $b_\tau$ on the exponent, motivated by convergence theory under contamination~\citep{wang2026survive}.
10	$\aeff$ correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$ (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}); limitations are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
11	
12	\paragraph{Stability ceiling.}
13	Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b) = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$~\citep{kish1965survey} decreases monotonically in $b$ (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
14	We require $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, yielding an upper bound $\bess$.
15	
16	\paragraph{Adaptive $\bstar$.}
17	Since $\aeff$ is non-decreasing and ESS is decreasing in $b$, the two constraints define an interval $[b_\tau, \bess]$.
18	The optimal exponent implements \emph{minimum intervention}:
19	\begin{equation}
20	  b^{*} = \begin{cases}
21	    0        & \text{if } \aeff(0) \geq \tau, \\
22	    b_\tau   & \text{if } b_\tau \leq \bess, \\
23	    \bess & \text{otherwise (stability precedence)},
24	  \end{cases}
25	  \label{eq:bstar}
26	\end{equation}
27	applying the smallest $b$ that achieves the quality floor.
28	Each batch falls into one of three regimes---clean, $\aeff$-binding, or ESS-binding---whose frequencies we analyze in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
29	Given $\bstar$, normalized weights $\pi_i = w_i(\bstar) / \sum_j w_j(\bstar)$ define the weighted loss $\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \pi_i \ell_i$; $\bstar$ is found via bisection (Algorithm~\ref{alg:bstar}, Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
30	Defaults: $\tau{=}0.7$, $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$; sensitivity in \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}.
